source.title: DiscrimLoss: A Universal Loss for Hard Samples and Incorrect Samples Discrimination
source.authors: Tingting Wu; Xiao Ding; Hao Zhang; Jin-Fang Gao; Min-Ji Tang; Li Du; Bing Qin; Ting Liu

page_placements.theme: Generalization peaks and stopping rules depend on training conditions

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests training and generalization under partially corrupted labels using a proposed loss and comparisons with cross-entropy and SuperLoss; it does not test completely random labels.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for manually corrupted labels, including training accuracy and test-curve behavior at 40% noise. Results cited from other studies are not included as rows. Table results are omitted where the flattened layout does not reliably associate values with conditions and models.
record.test_reason: The vanilla cross-entropy baseline directly measures fitting of randomly corrupted training labels: WideResNet-28-10 reaches 99.58% training accuracy at 40% symmetric noise. This tests the training-fit component of V4 using the same basic method and measure, although the paper primarily evaluates a mitigation method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors conclude that DiscrimLoss separates hard correct samples from incorrect samples, improves generalization, and suppresses noisy-label memorization. Their 60% reference describes expected fitting without memorizing corrupted labels, rather than a mathematical upper bound on training accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces DiscrimLoss and evaluates training with manually corrupted labels; it does not reproduce the original random-label memorization experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that DiscrimLoss test accuracy levels off after about 80 epochs while other methods show a downward trend under the tested CIFAR-100, 40% noise setting.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed 40% noise, CE and SuperLoss test accuracy declines late in training, while DiscrimLoss plateaus after about 80 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample-weighting objectives can reduce late-training deterioration in generalization under label noise.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code will be released upon publication.
record.problems: The directly relevant generalization analysis is limited to CIFAR-100 at 40% noise; test-curve values are only shown in a figure and described qualitatively. The paper does not test fully random labels.
record.rows_left_out: Tables III–VII report test metrics across noise levels and methods, but the supplied flattened layout does not reliably preserve all method-to-value associations; no rows were reconstructed from those tables.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, chance test performance, and fitting without architecture or hyperparameter changes.
Relative time to convergence on true and random labels, and convergence slowing across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across a corruption sweep extending to fully random labels, jointly with test error rising toward chance. The test-metric sweeps do not report corresponding training fits.
Controlled comparisons of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation, including generalization after their removal.

Directly established ordering of shared real-pattern learning and subsequent noise memorization under ordinary training. Aggregate test curves do not establish that ordering; the supplied flattened loss-distribution figures do not permit a reliable reading of it.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Modified-loss results qualify the tested training objective; they do not challenge the vanilla cross-entropy result. Tables III–VII are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment assigns completely random labels to the entire training set and tests whether standard networks fit them without changes.
No comparison measures time to fit random versus true labels or training time across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.

The study tests 40% corrupted labels in a CIFAR-100 generalization analysis and reports results on multiple manually corrupted datasets, but does not report a complete training-accuracy sweep from zero to all labels corrupted showing perfect fit at every noise level.
No experiment tests whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels or whether removing them impairs true-label generalization.
No experiment measures whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

relation.reason: The study reports its own measurements of corrupted-training-set fitting, including near-perfect fit under vanilla CE and suppressed fitting under sample-weighting objectives.

tranche.reason: The vanilla CE comparator uses randomly corrupted training labels and directly measures training accuracy, testing V4's fitting component with the same basic method and measure. The modified objectives supply additional scope qualifications.

source_check.notes: The 60% reference is source wording, not a valid universal training-accuracy ceiling. R1–R3 address fitting at one corruption fraction; R4–R6 describe epoch-dependent test behavior and do not establish V4's full corruption-response curve or V6's clean-versus-noisy learning order.
